keyVerseText: And if thou offer a meat offering of thy firstfruits unto the LORD, thou shalt offer for the meat offering of thy firstfruits green ears of corn dried by the fire, even corn beaten out of full ears.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun גֶּרֶשׂ (geres) originates from an unused root meaning "to husk," which suggests a process of separating or breaking down the grain from its protective outer layers. This etymological sense highlights the concept of something that has been physically crushed or beaten, emphasizing the tangible, concrete nature of the grain after processing rather than the grain in its whole form. This root meaning enriches the common English gloss of "beaten corn" by focusing on the transformation the grain undergoes to become usable, symbolizing refinement and preparation.
usageInScripture: The word גֶּרֶשׂ appears only twice in Scripture, consistently referring to grain that has been beaten or crushed, such as "even corn beaten" or "part of the beaten corn." This narrow range of usage underscores a specific agricultural product—grain that is no longer whole but has been processed into groats or grits. The consistency in translation reveals a clear and focused semantic field centered on the physical state of the grain after threshing and crushing, used especially in the context of offerings.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding גֶּרֶשׂ as "beaten corn" or crushed grain is theologically significant because it points to the idea of transformation and offering. In the sacrificial system, presenting grain in this processed form symbolizes giving God the fruit of labor that has been refined and prepared, reflecting a heart of dedication and surrender. This also anticipates the New Testament truth of Christ, who was 'crushed' for our iniquities, offering Himself as the perfect sacrifice. Thus, the word deepens our appreciation of the cost and holiness involved in worship and the offering of our lives to God.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 2:14 commands that if one offers a meat offering of firstfruits, it should include green ears of corn dried by fire and "even corn beaten out of full ears." The use of גֶּרֶשׂ here emphasizes the processed nature of the grain, highlighting the care and intentionality in preparing offerings to the LORD. This crushed grain symbolizes not only the physical preparation but also the spiritual readiness to present something refined and valuable to God, reminding believers that worship involves offering what has been thoughtfully and humbly prepared.
